original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: "Impression, Sunrise" (1872) - gave movement its name
final_text: Monet's Impression, Sunrise, shown in 1874, gave Impressionism its name; in 2014 astronomer Donald Olson dated its Le Havre harbour view to 13 November 1872, about 7:35 a.m.
source_note: Olson study for Marmottan 2014 exhibition catalogue

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: "Water Lilies" series (1896-1926) - 250 paintings at Giverny
final_text: Monet painted about 250 Water Lilies over the last three decades of his life at Giverny; the eight great murals opened at the Orangerie on 16 May 1927, months after his death.
source_note: approx. 250 oils; Orangerie opened 16 May 1927

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: "Haystacks" series - same subject, different light/seasons
final_text: In Moscow in 1896 Kandinsky saw a Monet Haystack and could not tell what it was until the catalogue told him; that painful non-recognition, he wrote, gave painting a fairy-tale power.
source_note: Kandinsky's own recollection of Moscow 1896 exhibition

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: "Rouen Cathedral" series - 30+ paintings of same facade
final_text: Monet painted Rouen Cathedral's west facade more than 30 times (1892-94); in 1892 he worked from the fitting room of Fernand Levy's lingerie shop, screened off after customers complained.
source_note: Rouen tourism office history of the Cathedrals series

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: "La Grenouillère" (1869) - with Renoir, proto-Impressionism
final_text: On 25 September 1869 Monet wrote to Bazille of a dream painting, the baths of La Grenouillere, with only 'bad sketches' done; Renoir painted the same Seine bathing spot beside him.
source_note: Met catalogue entry quoting Monet's letter to Bazille

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: Lived at Giverny 1883-1926, created famous gardens
final_text: In 1893 Monet bought land crossed by the Ru, an arm of the Epte, to dig his lily pond; local farmers protested that his strange water plants would poison their water and cattle.
source_note: Farmers' 1893 objections to Monet's water garden

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: Went nearly blind but kept painting
final_text: In January 1923 Dr Charles Coutela removed the cataract from Monet's right eye; with Zeiss Katral lenses Monet found his recent colours dull and began repainting canvases brighter.
source_note: Medical history of Monet's cataract surgery and lenses

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CLAUDE MONET (1840-1926) - The Father of Impressionism: Quote: "I want to paint the air"
final_text: On 7 October 1890, painting his grainstacks, Monet wrote to Gustave Geffroy that he was chasing 'instantaneity', above all the enveloppe, the same light spread over everything, as the sun set too fast.
source_note: Art Institute catalogue quotes Monet's letter to Geffroy

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: "Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette" (1876) - Parisian life
final_text: Renoir's smaller version of Bal du moulin de la Galette (1876) sold at Sotheby's New York on 17 May 1990 for $78.1 million to Ryoei Saito; the large one, Caillebotte's, is in the Orsay.
source_note: 1990 Sotheby's sale; Orsay version from Caillebotte

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: "Luncheon of the Boating Party" (1881) - friends at Chatou
final_text: Luncheon of the Boating Party (1880-81) is set at the Maison Fournaise, Chatou; Aline Charigot, his future wife, holds the dog; Duncan Phillips paid $125,000 for it in 1923.
source_note: Phillips Collection purchase 1923 and sitters

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: "Bathers" series - voluptuous nudes
final_text: Renoir spent about three years (1884-87) on The Large Bathers, now in Philadelphia, basing it partly on Girardon's 1672 lead relief The Bath of the Nymphs at Versailles.
source_note: Girardon relief source; Philadelphia Museum of Art

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: "La Loge" (1874) - theater box, fashionable woman
final_text: In La Loge (1874, Courtauld) the woman is Montmartre model Nini Lopez, nicknamed 'Gueule-de-Raie', the man Renoir's brother Edmond; Renoir sold it to pere Martin for 425 francs.
source_note: Sitters and 425-franc sale to pere Martin

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: Later developed "Ingresque" style - firmer forms
final_text: After an 1881-82 trip to Italy with Aline Charigot, struck by Raphael's Farnesina frescoes, Renoir turned to firm Ingres-like contours, his self-declared 'crisis of Impressionism'.
source_note: Clark Art Institute: Renoir's Italian journey

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: Painted despite crippling arthritis, brush strapped to hand
final_text: Renoir's brush was not strapped on: in Sacha Guitry's 1915 film he paints at 74 while his son Claude, 14, places the brush in his permanently clenched hand.
source_note: Guitry's 1915 film Ceux de chez nous

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › PIERRE-AUGUSTE RENOIR (1841-1919) - Joy and Sensuality: Quote: "Pain passes, but beauty remains"
final_text: Asked by Matisse why he kept painting despite crippling arthritis, Renoir reportedly answered: 'The pain passes, but the beauty remains.'
source_note: Wikiquote: attributed, reply to Matisse

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: "The Dance Class" series - ballet rehearsals
final_text: Degas's The Dance Class (1874-76) shows the old ballet master Jules Perrot, who had been ballet master of the Imperial Theatres in St Petersburg from 1849 to 1860.
source_note: Fitzwilliam Museum on Jules Perrot

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: "L'Absinthe" (1876) - café alienation
final_text: Degas's Dans un cafe (1875-76) posed actress Ellen Andree and engraver Marcellin Desboutin at the Nouvelle-Athenes; renamed L'Absinthe in London in 1893, it caused uproar.
source_note: Models, cafe, 1893 London renaming and scandal

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: "The Tub" series - women bathing
final_text: Degas told George Moore his bathing women were 'honest, simple folk' unaware of an audience: 'It is as if you looked through a key-hole' (Impressions and Opinions, 1891).
source_note: Quoted by George Moore, 1891

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: "At the Races" - horses, jockeys
final_text: Degas copied horse positions from Muybridge's 1887 Animal Locomotion photographs, counterproofing drawings to see both sides, and used them for his first bronze horses in motion.
source_note: Orsay notes Muybridge influence on Degas horses

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: "Little Dancer of Fourteen Years" (1881) - sculpture
final_text: Little Dancer Aged Fourteen, shown in wax in 1881 with a real tulle tutu, silk ribbon and hair, was modelled by Marie van Goethem; the bronzes were cast only around 1922.
source_note: National Gallery of Art holds the original wax

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: Not strictly Impressionist - called himself "Realist"
final_text: Degas rejected the label 'Impressionist', preferring to be called a Realist or an Independent, though he helped organise the group shows of 1874-86.
source_note: Newfields artist bio on Degas's preferred labels

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: Master of pastels, unusual angles, cropped compositions
final_text: Degas layered his pastels using a secret fixative from his friend Luigi Chialiva, a chemist-trained painter; a casein-based fixative was patented in the US in 1899 by Chialiva and Dupont.
source_note: Thyssen technical study of Degas's At the Milliner's

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › EDGAR DEGAS (1834-1917) - Movement and Modern Life: Quote: "Art is not what you see, but what you make others see"
final_text: The sourced Degas line is 'Drawing is not what you see but what you must make others see' (Shop-Talk of Edgar Degas); the popular 'Art is not what you see' version is a paraphrase.
source_note: Wikiquote: Shop-Talk of Edgar Degas, Gammell 1961

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CAMILLE PISSARRO (1830-1903) - The Patriarch: Only artist in all 8 Impressionist exhibitions
final_text: Pissarro was the only artist to show at all eight Paris Impressionist exhibitions, from 1874 to 1886.
source_note: Only artist in all eight exhibitions

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CAMILLE PISSARRO (1830-1903) - The Patriarch: Taught Cézanne, Gauguin, Van Gogh
final_text: Pissarro mentored Cezanne and Gauguin, who called him 'one of my masters'; Cezanne listed himself as 'pupil of Pissarro' in Aix in 1902; for Van Gogh, Pissarro suggested Auvers and Dr Gachet in 1890.
source_note: Cezanne catalogue raisonne: 1902 Salon Aixois entry

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CAMILLE PISSARRO (1830-1903) - The Patriarch: "Boulevard Montmartre" series - Paris streets from above
final_text: Between February and April 1897 Pissarro painted 14 views of the boulevard Montmartre from his room at the Grand Hotel de Russie, in snow, rain, fog, sunlight and once at night.
source_note: National Gallery: The Boulevard Montmartre at Night

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CAMILLE PISSARRO (1830-1903) - The Patriarch: Rural scenes of Pontoise, Éragny
final_text: Pissarro rented his Eragny house for eight years, then bought it on 19 July 1892 at his wife Julie's insistence, with 15,000 francs borrowed from Monet.
source_note: Drouot on the Eragny house purchase

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CAMILLE PISSARRO (1830-1903) - The Patriarch: Briefly adopted Pointillism (1886-1888)
final_text: Introduced to Seurat in October 1885, Pissarro, nearly 30 years older, adopted the dot technique, showed with Seurat and Signac in 1886, and abandoned it by about 1890.
source_note: Met essay on Neo-Impressionism; 1886 exhibition

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › CAMILLE PISSARRO (1830-1903) - The Patriarch: Quote: "Blessed are they who see beautiful things"
final_text: Late in life Cezanne spoke with particular tenderness of 'the humble and colossal Pissarro', and called him 'a father for me, a man to consult and a little like the good Lord'.
source_note: Rewald, History of Impressionism, quoting Cezanne

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › BERTHE MORISOT (1841-1895) - The First Lady: First woman in Impressionist group
final_text: Berthe Morisot was the only woman in the first Impressionist exhibition of 1874 and showed in seven of the eight, missing only 1879 after the birth of her daughter Julie.
source_note: Only woman 1874; seven of eight shows

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › BERTHE MORISOT (1841-1895) - The First Lady: "The Cradle" (1872) - sister watching baby
final_text: The Cradle (1872) shows Morisot's sister Edma watching her baby Blanche; it failed to sell at the 1874 exhibition, stayed in the family, and entered the Louvre in 1930.
source_note: Unsold 1874; acquired by Louvre 1930

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › BERTHE MORISOT (1841-1895) - The First Lady: "Summer's Day" (1879) - women in boat
final_text: Summer's Day (1879, National Gallery London) shows two women in a rowing boat on the lake of the Bois de Boulogne; it was shown at the 1880 Impressionist exhibition.
source_note: National Gallery: Lane Bequest 1917

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › BERTHE MORISOT (1841-1895) - The First Lady: Married Édouard Manet's brother Eugène
final_text: In 1874, the year of the first Impressionist show, Berthe Morisot married Eugene Manet, younger brother of Edouard Manet, who had painted her many times.
source_note: Married Eugene Manet 1874

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › BERTHE MORISOT (1841-1895) - The First Lady: Delicate brushwork, domestic scenes, gardens
final_text: When Berthe Morisot died in 1895, her death certificate described her as 'sans profession', no profession.
source_note: Death certificate listed no profession

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › BERTHE MORISOT (1841-1895) - The First Lady: Quote: "I don't think any man would ever treat a woman as his equal"
final_text: Morisot wrote in her notebook in 1890: 'I don't think there has ever been a man who treated a woman as an equal, and that's all I would have asked, for I know I'm worth as much as they.'
source_note: AWARE biography quoting 1890 notebook

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › ALFRED SISLEY (1839-1899) - Pure Landscape: Most consistent Impressionist - never changed style
final_text: In 1893-94 Sisley painted the church of Notre-Dame at Moret about a dozen times from nearly the same spot, in different seasons and weather, his most deliberate series.
source_note: Moret Church series, 12-14 canvases

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › ALFRED SISLEY (1839-1899) - Pure Landscape: "Flood at Port-Marly" (1876) - water reflections
final_text: When the Seine flooded Port-Marly in spring 1876 Sisley painted several views; Boat in the Flood was bought by Count Isaac de Camondo at the Tavernier sale on 6 March 1900.
source_note: Flood series 1876; Orsay provenance via Camondo

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › ALFRED SISLEY (1839-1899) - Pure Landscape: "Snow at Louveciennes" series
final_text: Not a series: Snow at Louveciennes (1878, Musee d'Orsay) is one of many snow scenes Sisley painted, a snowy lane narrowing into the distance with a single small figure.
source_note: Orsay painting, 1878, 61 x 50.5 cm

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › ALFRED SISLEY (1839-1899) - Pure Landscape: English parents, lived in France
final_text: Born in Paris to a British merchant father, Sisley stayed British all his life: his 1898 application for French citizenship was refused and a second was overtaken by his final illness.
source_note: 1898 naturalisation attempts failed

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › ALFRED SISLEY (1839-1899) - Pure Landscape: Died poor, prices rose after death
final_text: Sisley died of throat cancer at Moret on 29 January 1899; on 1 May 1899 Monet's benefit sale at Galerie Georges Petit raised 145,000 francs for his children.
source_note: Death and Monet's benefit auction

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › MARY CASSATT (1844-1926) - American in Paris: Only American in Impressionist exhibitions
final_text: Mary Cassatt was the only American officially associated with the Impressionists; Degas invited her to exhibit with them in 1877, after her Salon submissions were rejected.
source_note: Only American; Degas invitation 1877

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › MARY CASSATT (1844-1926) - American in Paris: "The Child's Bath" (1893) - mother and child
final_text: Cassatt's The Child's Bath (1893, Art Institute of Chicago) followed her study of the 1890 Paris exhibition of Japanese prints: high viewpoint, flat patterns, cropped figures.
source_note: The Child's Bath 1893 and Japanese influence

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › MARY CASSATT (1844-1926) - American in Paris: "Little Girl in a Blue Armchair" (1878)
final_text: Degas worked on the background of Cassatt's Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878) and supplied the model, a friend's daughter; the American jury of the 1878 World's Fair rejected it.
source_note: Cassatt's letter to Vollard; infrared confirms Degas

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › MARY CASSATT (1844-1926) - American in Paris: Influenced by Japanese prints
final_text: After a major Paris exhibition of Japanese masters in 1890, Cassatt made a set of colour drypoint and aquatint prints in 1891, among her most original works.
source_note: 1890 Japanese exhibition; 1891 colour prints

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › MARY CASSATT (1844-1926) - American in Paris: Helped American collectors buy Impressionists
final_text: Cassatt urged her friend Louisine Havemeyer to buy her first artwork, a Degas pastel; the Havemeyer bequest after 1929 gave the Met nearly 2,000 works.
source_note: First purchase a Degas pastel; Met bequest

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › MARY CASSATT (1844-1926) - American in Paris: Quote: "I have touched with a sense of art some people"
final_text: Of Degas's pastels in a Paris dealer's window around 1875, Cassatt said: 'I used to go and flatten my nose against that window and absorb all I could of his art. It changed my life.'
source_note: Mathews, Mary Cassatt: A Life (1998), p.114

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › GUSTAVE CAILLEBOTTE (1848-1894) - The Collector: "Paris Street; Rainy Day" (1877) - geometric precision
final_text: Paris Street; Rainy Day (1877) shows today's Place de Dublin, where rue de Saint-Petersbourg meets rue de Moscou; Caillebotte showed it at the 1877 Impressionist show he helped fund.
source_note: Location, 1877 show; AIC bought 1964

original: ART HISTORY - Complete Guide to Impressionism and Beyond › GUSTAVE CAILLEBOTTE (1848-1894) - The Collector: "The Floor Scrapers" (1875) - workers
final_text: The Floor Scrapers (1875), set in Caillebotte's flat at 77 rue de Miromesnil, was rejected by the 1875 Salon as vulgar, then shown at the 1876 Impressionist exhibition.
source_note: Salon rejection 1875; second exhibition 1876
